title: Agent Q: Advanced Reasoning and Learning for Autonomous AI Agents

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to enable LLM web agents to autonomously improve from their own experience with limited supervision, overcoming compounding errors and limited exploration of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert demonstrations. Paper [6] discusses LLMs self-improving at web agent tasks, specifically addressing challenges in training agents to navigate complex environments with limited data. This aligns with the same objective of enabling autonomous improvement in web agents. Paper [9] also addresses the limitations of LLMs in multi-step reasoning, planning, and using environmental feedback, which overlaps with the goal of overcoming compounding errors and limited exploration. Both papers share the same problem-class level objective.

### Mechanism
The contribution introduces the Agent Q framework, which combines guided Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) over web pages to collect trajectories, an AI self-critique/process-supervision model for ranking candidate actions, and iterative step-level fine-tuning via an off-policy variant of DPO that learns from both successful and failed trajectories. Paper [5] introduces Language Agent Tree Search (LATS), which integrates MCTS into LLMs for reasoning, acting, and planning, leveraging in-context learning and environmental feedback. This is substantively equivalent to the use of MCTS for trajectory collection and decision-making in Agent Q. Paper [21] discusses step-level reward models for reasoning, which aligns with the process-supervision model in Agent Q that provides step-level feedback. Paper [22] introduces Model-induced Process Supervision (MiPS), which uses a verifier to evaluate intermediate steps, similar to the self-critique model in Agent Q. Paper [27] discusses Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF), which uses AI-generated feedback for iterative improvement, aligning with the off-policy fine-tuning mechanism in Agent Q. These papers collectively cover the mechanism.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates Agent Q using WebShop and OpenTable benchmarks, reporting success rates and improvements over baselines like RFT and DPO. Paper [9] evaluates tree search algorithms for LM agents on web automation tasks, which matches the evaluation design of using benchmarks for web navigation tasks. Paper [28] validates domain-general automatic evaluators on benchmarks for digital agents, which aligns with the use of benchmark-based evaluation for web agents. Paper [6] evaluates LLMs on web agent tasks, which also matches the evaluation design. These papers collectively cover the evaluation design.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of autonomous LLM web agents and decision-making. Paper [6] explicitly addresses LLMs acting as agents in web environments, which is the same application area. Paper [9] focuses on LM agents performing decision-making tasks such as web automation, which is substantively equivalent. Paper [28] discusses improving agents for web navigation and device control, which is also within the same domain. These papers cover the domain.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves applying Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) at test time, using the fine-tuned Agent Q model as the action-proposal distribution and the critic for action ordering. Paper [6] introduces MCTS in a multiagent path-planning domain, and paper [9] reviews MCTS applications, including its use in sequential decision problems. Paper [14] describes combining MCTS with trained policies for self-play optimization, which is conceptually equivalent to using MCTS with a fine-tuned model for decision-making. These prior works demonstrate substantively equivalent mechanisms: leveraging MCTS with learned models for action selection and ordering.

The evaluation design uses benchmarks (WebShop and OpenTable) to measure agent success rates with and without test-time search. Paper [16] introduces AgentQuest, a modular benchmark framework for evaluating LLM agents, which aligns with the evaluation design of benchmarking agent performance. Paper [22] introduces WebCanvas, another evaluation framework for web agents, which similarly measures success rates in dynamic web environments. Both prior papers use benchmark-based evaluation designs, making the evaluation facet covered.

Paper [1] explicitly addresses autonomous LLM agents performing web automation tasks, and paper [22] focuses on web agents in online environments. Both papers operate in the same general application area of autonomous LLM web agents, covering the domain facet.
